newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Bruton sees some progress on EU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bruton sees some progress on EU budget pact.

text.p: European Union countries are in the process of narrowing their differences on a budget discipline pact and may reach an agreement in talks in Dublin later this week, Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Tuesday.
Bruton, whose country holds the EU presidency, said French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl had made progress on the pact in summit talks in Germany on Monday.
"The president and the chancellor did make some progress on the matter but it is not resolved yet," he told a news conference after a meeting with Chirac.
He said he hoped finance ministers would agree a political declaration enshrining the stability pact at a meeting in Dublin on Thursday ahead of an EU summit there on Friday and Saturday.
"I hope the finance ministers will be able to give us the text of a political declaration," he said.

"What we are seeing here is a position where people are coming closer together hopefully but until they actually come together and shake on it, they all still have their starting positions on the table," he said.
But he left open the possibility of failure in Dublin. "There are strong arguments for completing this business before the Dublin summit... But if we don't, there is no deadline."

Earlier this year, officials had said they expected the Dublin summit to provide a political agreement on the pact, which would fine members of European monetary union if they ran up big budget deficits after the launch of the new euro in 1999.
But the talks have foundered on German insistence that special circumstances which could exempt countries from fines be numerically defined. Other countries want a looser definition.
While officials stress this is only a tiny part of the accord, the row over "temporary and exceptional circumstances" threatens to derail the smooth march to monetary union.

Germany, fearing any erosion in the credibility of the new euro, wants a watertight accord. But its insistence on getting its own way on every detail of the pact has raised hackles among its EU partners, particularly in France.
Bruton said Germany continued to insist that there should be numerical definitions of exceptional circumstances.

"The German requirement is that if certain figures are not on the table reflecting reality...you don't have an exceptional circumstance and you don't have the possibility of not initiating a procedure which might ultimately lead to a fine.

"The position of other member states is that they agree there should be figures which define what is exceptional for the purpose of not having a fine. They agree those figures should be taken into account...but they don't want it to be absolutely automatic. They want a margin for appreciation," he said.

"The solution lies in defining or constraining the margin for appreciation," he added. For example, one could limit the right to make this judgement to EU finance ministers rather than extending it to the European Commission, he said.
"It all hinges on assurances that the exceptional circumstances exception will not be used in a politically easy way," he said.
A potential compromise appears to be shaping up around an agreement that countries whose economies shrink by 1.5 percent would automatically be exempt from fines.
Germany had originally insisted on a drop of two percent.

At less severe levels of recession, countries which had undergone four consecutive quarters of negative growth could be included in the automatic exemption, while a recession falling short of either of these measurements would be left to ministerial judgement, within pre-defined guidelines, some officials suggest.

"You can have 1.5 percent of a fall and a fall in four quarters, or you can have 1.5 percent or a fall in four quarters, or you can have 1.5 percent of a fall and/or a fall in four quarters," Bruton said.
"Nobody is disagreeing with figures being in the declaration," Bruton said.
